# A full local convex-body neighborhood of the triangle Lorentz inequalities

This is an ordinary planar theorem for a fixed source and fixed three
normals. It has no polygon-count or smoothness assumption. It does not
prove the inequalities for bodies outside the neighborhood, nor preserve
compatibility with neighboring mixed fibers.

## 1. Statement and exact proved inputs

Fix source zero and spanning normals v_1+v_2+v_3=0. For a convex body K
containing zero in its interior define

    k=|K|, Q_i=|K intersect{v_i.x>=0}|,
    sigma_i=H_1(K intersect{v_i.x=0})/||v_i||,
    M=sum_i Q_i/sigma_i,
    f_i=2sqrt(k Q_i)/(sigma_i M),
    Phi_i=f_i+(f_j+f_l)^2/4.

Let T be a triangle whose three source cuts strictly isolate its three
distinct vertices.

**Theorem.** There is a Hausdorff neighborhood of T such that every
convex body K in the neighborhood satisfies Phi_i(K)<=2 for all three
rows. Every nontriangular K in that neighborhood has all three rows
strict. The source remains in the interior of every body considered.

The inputs, each already proved independently, are:

1. The actual triangle Lorentz inequalities.
2. At a triangle tight at a selected row, an outward one-point ear over
   ANY edge, with ANY fixed interior peak, has strictly negative first
   variation at that row, including cut-ray crossing peaks. The sources
   are `candidate 146226205b30285c`
   and `candidate 8e1d01c76d1a2560`.
   Their ear functional is continuous in the triangle and peak parameter;
   the explicit matching clipping formulas also prove this in Section2
   of `candidate 3be9fc800740b04a`.
3. The exact six-sector replacement theorem in
   `candidate be9098c627b40217`.
   It preserves every sector area, six ray endpoints, chosen actual
   endpoint support lines, total area, three caps and three sections,
   using the six endpoints and one positive-coordinate auxiliary in
   each sector. In endpoint coordinates P,Q that auxiliary is

       V=u P+v Q,   u,v>0,   u+v=2|K intersect sector|/det(P,Q),

   and lies in the two actual endpoint support halfplanes.

The replacement theorem is used as an exact finite-data theorem, not as
an assumption that the original body is polygonal. We first prove the
additional convergence control it requires here.

## 2. Every chosen six-sector replacement converges to T

Suppose K tends to T in Hausdorff distance. Fix r>0 with r times the unit
disk contained in T. The support-function bound for Hausdorff distance
implies, for distance epsilon<r,

    (1-epsilon/r)T subset K subset (1+epsilon/r)T.       (1)

Indeed h_T>=r on unit normals and |h_K-h_T|<=epsilon. These inclusions
keep the source interior. They also prove convergence of all six ray
endpoints, all six sector areas, the three cap areas and the sections:
dilations about zero preserve every sector, ray and source halfplane.
Write P_s^0 for the fixed six ray endpoints of T and P_s for those of K.

Each P_s^0 lies in the relative interior of one triangle edge. Choose
ANY actual supporting line of K at P_s, and normalize its linear form
ell_s so that ell_s(P_s)=1 and K subset{ell_s<=1}. These forms converge
to the unique normalized support form of T at P_s^0. Here is the full
compactness justification. For sufficiently small epsilon, K contains
(r/2) times the unit disk, so ||ell_s||<=2/r. Every subsequential limit
supports T at P_s^0, by (1) and endpoint convergence. The supporting
line of a triangle at an edge-interior point is unique. Thus all limit
forms agree, which proves convergence for every choice of the supports.

Apply the exact replacement theorem using these supports and call its
polygon P. There are three unique-signature sectors containing the old
triangle vertices and three intervening double-signature sectors.

In a unique sector, use its two endpoint vectors as coordinates. The
limiting endpoint wedge is

    W={u,v>=0: u+p v<=1, q u+v<=1},

where p,q<1 and D=1-pq>0. To check the latter sign without a
genericity assumption, the actual triangle vertex has positive
coordinates (u,v) on both support lines, so
(1-pq)u=1-p>0. Its additional vertex is

    E=((1-p)/D,(1-q)/D),

and it represents the corresponding vertex of T. The whole sector of
T equals this wedge: its four vertices zero, the two ray endpoints and
the triangle vertex all lie in T, and the two incident triangle facets
bound it. Hence the limiting area condition is u+v=E_1+E_2.

The coefficients of every replacement auxiliary are positive and have
bounded sum by its exact area formula and the nonzero limiting endpoint
determinant. Any limiting coefficient pair is therefore nonnegative,
satisfies the two wedge inequalities, and has sum E_1+E_2. The positive
linear combination of those inequalities with coefficients

    (1-q)/D and (1-p)/D

is precisely u+v<=E_1+E_2. Equality forces BOTH original inequalities
to be equalities, so the limiting pair is E. Therefore each unique-sector
auxiliary converges to its corresponding original triangle vertex.
This argument fixes its tangential coordinate as well as its area.

In a double sector the limiting triangle sector is its core triangle,
of area det(P_s^0,P_(s+1)^0)/2. Thus the positive auxiliary coefficients
satisfy u+v tending to1. Every limit auxiliary lies on the fixed bridge
segment [P_s^0,P_(s+1)^0], strictly within one old triangle edge. No
convergence to one particular point on that segment is asserted or needed.

It follows that P tends to T in Hausdorff distance. More precisely,
three of its auxiliary points converge to the old vertices, while every
other point in its at-most-twelve-point construction lies near one of
the three compact bridge segments. This conclusion holds for every
allowed choice of endpoint supports and replacement auxiliaries, not
merely for a specially selected convergent subsequence.

## 3. A nearby inner triangle removes endpoint concentration

Let V_1,V_2,V_3 be the unique-sector auxiliaries and set

    T_0=conv{V_1,V_2,V_3}.

For sufficiently small epsilon they are genuine exposed vertices of P.
To see this, choose at each old vertex a fixed linear functional strictly
maximized there on the finite union of the other old vertices and all
three old bridge segments. The gap is positive by compactness. The
convergence just proved preserves that gap. In particular T_0 is a
nearby strict-incidence triangle containing the source, and T_0 subset P.

All remaining construction points lie close to their assigned old bridge
segment. Relative to T_0, their coordinate along that edge stays in a
fixed interval [2kappa,1-2kappa], with kappa>0; their normal displacement
tends uniformly to zero. Also, in the barycentric coordinates of T_0,
each such point has its two coordinates belonging to that edge bounded
below by a fixed number c>0; only its opposite coordinate can be negative,
and that coordinate is at least -delta with delta tending to zero.

For delta<c, no point of the whole convex hull P has two negative
barycentric coordinates. Indeed group the construction points by their
assigned opposite edge. If a convex combination had coordinates i and j
both negative, and a_i,a_j were its total weights on the corresponding
two groups, one would have

    -delta a_i+c a_j<0,    -delta a_j+c a_i<0.

Contributions of the other group and of triangle vertices are
nonnegative and were only dropped. Neither weight can vanish; multiplying
the strict inequalities gives c^2<delta^2, a contradiction.

Therefore the three parts of P outside T_0 are disjoint edge ears. The
closed part outside any one edge is exactly the convex hull of that edge
and the construction vertices outside it: intersecting hull edges with
the base line produces only points of the base segment, since two
negative barycentric coordinates are impossible. This also proves that
no hidden joining piece is assigned twice.

For an oriented edge [A,B] of T_0 use coordinates

    x=A+s(B-A)+h w,

where w is the outward 90-degree rotation of B-A divided by |B-A|^2,
so |det(B-A,w)|=1 and the absolute Jacobian is1. The corresponding ear is exactly

    0<=s<=1,   0<=h<=h_e(s),

for a nonnegative concave polygonal roof h_e with h_e(0)=h_e(1)=0.
Every nontrivial breakpoint is in [kappa,1-kappa], by the location of
all the added construction points. Write H_e=max h_e and
E_e=integral_0^1 h_e(s)ds for its area. Uniformly,

    H_e/2<=E_e<=H_e,    Lip(h_e)<=H_e/kappa.             (2)

The first inequality follows because the unit-base tent through a
maximal point lies below the concave roof. For the second, the first
and last linear slopes have absolute value at most H_e/kappa, and
all intermediate slopes lie between them. Both H_e and E_e tend to
zero uniformly; there are only three ears.

## 4. Actual simultaneous clipping errors are small relative to ear area

We give the estimates across roof knots explicitly. The constants below
are uniform for T_0 in a sufficiently small coordinate neighborhood of T.
All its relevant edge-crossing slopes are bounded away from zero.

For a cap whose cutting line crosses an edge at s_0, its affine margin
in the displayed coordinates is

    Delta(s-s_0)+b h,      Delta!=0.

The ideal first-order area change is integral h_e over the captured
subinterval of the base. The actual indicator can differ from this
step indicator only where |s-s_0|<=|b/Delta|H_e. Its area is therefore
at most C H_e^2. This proves the area-error estimate even if a cutting
line crosses a roof vertex.

Along the actual cutting line s=s_0-(b/Delta)h, its added section ends
at the unique solution h_* of

    h_*=h_e(s_0-(b/Delta)h_*).

The solution lies in[0,H_e]. For small H_e the argument stays in(0,1),
and the right side minus h has strictly negative increments: its
Lipschitz slope contribution is at most |b/Delta|H_e/kappa<1/2.
It is nonnegative at0 and nonpositive at H_e. Thus existence and
uniqueness follow without differentiating at a knot. Moreover

    |h_*-h_e(s_0)|<=C H_e^2.

The coarea length increment is h_*/|Delta|, because the coordinate
Jacobian is1. Its error from the ideal h_e(s_0)/|Delta| is also at most
C H_e^2. The cap belonging to the opposite triangle vertex is strictly
negative on the entire small ear and has no increment. The two endpoint
extensions of any source chord from different ears are disjoint and add.

Let D(K) denote the seven-component data vector
(k,Q_1,Q_2,Q_3,sigma_1,sigma_2,sigma_3). Let L_e(h) be the linear ideal
data increment just described: area integral h, cap subinterval
integrals, and section values h(s_0)/|Delta|. Summing the actual ears,

    D(P)-D(T_0)=sum_e L_e(h_e)+R,
    ||R||<=C delta_0 E,
    ||D(P)-D(T_0)||<=C E,                              (3)

where E=sum E_e and delta_0=max H_e. Indeed H_e^2<=2delta_0 E_e by(2).
The linear section values are bounded by C H_e<=2C E_e, and all other
linear increments are bounded by ear area. This is a relative-error
estimate; a bare O(delta_0^2) would not suffice when ears concentrate.

## 5. Positive tent decomposition and the strict area margin

Fix a row i tight at T. On a sufficiently small positive compact raw-data
neighborhood, Phi_i is C^2 with bounded first and second derivatives.
This follows directly from its displayed formula: all k,Q_i,sigma_i,M
are bounded away from zero there. Taylor's formula and(3) give

    Phi_i(P)-Phi_i(T_0)
       =sum_e grad Phi_i(D(T_0)).L_e(h_e)+O(delta_0 E).  (4)

The quadratic Taylor error is also of this form, since E<=3delta_0.
The constants do not depend on the number of roof vertices or on which
roof knots are met by the source cuts.

For t in(0,1), let T_t(s) be the unit-height tent, linear from0 to its
peak at t and then to0 at1. A concave polygonal roof with breakpoints t_r
has the exact representation

    h_e=sum_r a_r T_(t_r),
    a_r=t_r(1-t_r)(left slope-right slope)>=0,
    sum_r a_r=2E_e.                                   (5)

To verify it, both sides have the same derivative jump at every knot,
then their difference is affine; the zero endpoint values make that
affine difference zero. Every t_r lies in[kappa,1-kappa].

For each edge, the functional

    grad Phi_i(D(T_0)).L_e(T_t)

is exactly the actual first derivative of its outward triangular ear
with that peak. It is continuous in T_0 and t, including the ray-crossing
values, by the proved formulas cited in Section1 (or by the matching
linear integrals and evaluations in Section4). At T it is strictly
negative at every such interior peak. On the compact set of three edges
and t in[kappa,1-kappa], its negative has a positive minimum. Hence for
some c_0>0, throughout a sufficiently small triangle neighborhood,

    grad Phi_i(D(T_0)).L_e(T_t)<=-c_0.                  (6)

Combining(4)--(6),

    Phi_i(P)-Phi_i(T_0)<=-2c_0 E+C delta_0 E.

The convergence in Sections2--3 lets us impose C delta_0<c_0 uniformly.
Thus

    Phi_i(P)<=Phi_i(T_0)-c_0 E<=2-c_0 E.               (7)

The last inequality is the actual triangle theorem. Exact replacement
preserves D, so Phi_i(K)=Phi_i(P), proving the selected row bound for
all convex bodies in the resulting Hausdorff neighborhood.

## 6. Strictness for every nontriangle and scope of the theorem

If E>0, equation(7) is strict. If E=0, then P=T_0. Each retained ray
endpoint lies in the relative interior of its corresponding edge of
T_0. The replacement theorem retains its chosen actual support line of
K. A triangle has only its edge line as a supporting line at such a
point. Hence the three edge halfplanes of T_0 also contain K, so
K subset T_0. Their areas agree by exact replacement. A proper closed
convex subset of a full-dimensional convex body has smaller volume
(strict separation supplies a positive-volume missing cap). Thus
K=T_0 is a triangle. This proves strictness for every nontriangular K.

Apply the argument to each tight row of T. Any row initially strict
remains strict in a small neighborhood, because(1) gives continuity of
its cap, section and total-area data. Intersect the finitely many
neighborhoods. This proves all parts of the theorem.

The proof supplies a full neighborhood of each fixed strict-incidence
triangle, but no uniform neighborhood over degenerating triangles or
cuts approaching their vertices. The exact replacement need not retain
compatibility with other fibers and has only been used to prove an
ordinary functional inequality for the original K, whose recorded data
it preserves. No global minimizer, polygonal approximation preserving
mixed fibers, or general-body Lorentz theorem is being assumed.
